messages.author: Dozer
messages.content: In this Guide I will go over what advanced creators who go for depth on interactions should be using. This will explain how character backends actually function along with how LLM's behave with the backend and why token efficiency builds more sustainable RP

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Step 1 — Image
Your image is visual.
It shows users what your character looks like. It does not need to carry your character's personality, lore, or behavioral instructions.
Don't waste your character definition describing what the image already shows.
Step 2 — Greeting
The greeting is where you set the world and start the scene.
Use it to establish:
The setting
The situation
The relationship between the characters
Relevant immediate history
The tone
What is happening when the conversation begins
Think of the greeting as the opening scene of the RP, not an introduction to the character.
Never speak for the user.
You can give the user a logical starting action:
The door opens as you step into the apartment.
But don't write:
You walk into the apartment, drop your bag on the floor, and smile at Sarah.
And never write dialogue for them:
"Hey, Sarah. How was your day?"
The user controls their own character.
Your character controls your character.
The user controls theirs.
The persona the user equips exists specifically to provide their character's identity, personality, appearance, and behavior.
A good greeting should give the user something to respond to.
Don't end with an empty introduction:
"Hi, I'm Sarah. Nice to meet you!"
Give them a situation:
Sarah looks up from the kitchen counter as the apartment door opens. She's been waiting for you for nearly an hour, and the untouched dinner sitting between you tells you this isn't going to be a normal evening.
"You're late."
Now the user has a world, a relationship, tension, and an immediate reason to respond—without the creator taking control of their character.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Step 3 — Personality
⚠️This is the most important field in the character builder.⚠️

Personality is where you define how the character thinks, behaves, reacts, speaks, and what rules govern them. It is also the only field where you should put behavioral machinery.

You have 4,000 characters available. That does not mean you should use 4,000 characters. More information is not automatically better. Every unnecessary detail consumes context that could otherwise be used during the actual conversation.

What belongs here?
Focus on information the LLM actually needs to consistently portray the character:
Core personality traits
Behavioral patterns
Speech style
Motivations and priorities
Likes/dislikes that affect behavior
How they react to specific situations
Character-specific rules
Relationship behavior
Boundaries and persistent behaviors
Behavioral machinery
If your character has a mechanic that needs to remain active throughout the RP, put it here.

For example:
When challenged, she becomes defensive rather than apologetic.
She attempts to regain control of conversations through sarcasm and intimidation.
She does not immediately abandon her established goals because of a single user response.

These are useful because they tell the model how to behave, rather than simply giving it trivia about the character.
Don't confuse detail with usefulness
A common mistake is filling the Personality field with everything that makes the character interesting.

A three-paragraph biography, childhood history, favorite foods, extensive physical description, and ten paragraphs of lore may make the character look detailed, but that does not mean the LLM will consistently use those details.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Ask yourself:
"Will this information change how the character responds during conversation?"
If the answer is no, it probably doesn't belong in Personality.
Write for the LLM, not for the character's résumé.
Keep machinery out of Scenario
Do not use Scenario to store behavioral rules or character mechanics.
Scenario has a different job.
Personality = who the character is and how they behave.
Scenario = what is happening right now.
If a character always becomes jealous when another woman receives attention, that belongs in Personality.
If another woman is currently standing in the room and receiving the user's attention, that belongs in Scenario.
Keeping these separate makes the character easier for the model to understand and gives you much more control over the opening situation.
The goal
A good Personality field should give the model a compact behavioral blueprint, not an encyclopedia.
Use the space for things the character needs to remember. Don't fill the space simply because it exists.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Step 4 — Advanced: Scenario & Example Dialogue
Scenario
Keep it short.
Scenario describes the current state of the RP when the conversation begins.
It should answer:
Where are we?
What is happening right now?
What does the character currently know?
What is the immediate situation?
That's it.
Your Greeting already establishes the opening scene, so the Scenario should reinforce that context rather than retell it.
Don't use Scenario for:
Personality
Character rules
Behavioral machinery
Backstory
Long-term lore
Instructions that belong in Personality
A well-written greeting + a short Scenario gives the model enough information to understand where the RP starts without spending unnecessary context.
Example:
Sheena has been dating {{user}} for several months. Today she brought her boss home under the excuse of a "performance review." She expects {{user}} to remain unaware of what is happening.
That's enough.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Example Dialogue — Teach Behavior, Not Volume
Example Dialogue is the second most important field.
You don't need to use all 4,000 characters. More examples do not automatically create a better character.
Use short, purposeful examples that show the model how the character behaves.
You don't need special formatting such as <Start>.
Numbered examples are fine.
You can include user actions, but never write dialogue for the user.
Demonstrate the character's speech, actions, reactions, internal thoughts, and contradictions.
Use examples to show behavior that is difficult to explain with a simple rule.
Most importantly, ladder your examples.
Show the character:
Initially — their baseline personality and attitude.
~10 messages in — still maintaining that personality.
~20 messages in — personality remains intact as the RP develops.
40+ messages in — the same character still exists deep into the RP.
You can use more than four examples. Four is simply enough to demonstrate the concept.
The goal is not to fill the character limit.
Short examples give the LLM behavioral anchors. Laddered examples give it somewhere to go as the user changes the situation.
Instead of spending 4,000 characters explaining everything your character could do, give the model a handful of strong examples showing how the character responds to different user input.
That leaves room for the RP itself to develop rather than trying to pre-write the entire character's behavior.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Closing: Compress, Don't Bloat

This is probably the most antithetical idea in this entire guide:
⚠️You should be trying to compress your character into as few tokens as possible.⚠️

A 4,000-character field is not an invitation to use 4,000 characters.
A bloated character can produce beautiful prose, detailed descriptions, and an impressive backstory for the first several interactions — and then fall apart because the LLM has very little useful behavioral information left to work with once the opening context fades.

Behavioral Machinery is lean, precision engineering for your bot. It gives the LLM behavioral rules, reactions, motivations, and patterns that allow it to drive the story from user input rather than following a predetermined railroad.
The railroad feels impressive while you're on it.

But once the track runs out, the story is over.
With less powerful models, that railroad can run out in three messages.

Build your character so the LLM has room to respond, adapt, and create.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
How an LLM Actually Uses Your Character
The easiest way to understand an LLM is to imagine a person sitting at a desk with a filing cabinet.
Your character's backend is the filing cabinet. It contains information about the character: personality, behavioral rules, scenario, examples, and other information provided to the model.
But the LLM isn't sitting there with every file spread across its desk at all times.
It has a limited workspace.
The information currently available to the model is its active context.
The filing cabinet can contain information without that information necessarily being on the desk.
As the conversation continues, more material gets placed on the desk:
•Character information
•Scenario
•Conversation history
•User messages
•Previous responses
•Memories or retrieved information
•System instructions
•The space required to generate the next response
But the desk has a finite size.
Eventually, something has to be pushed off.
That's context loss.

The character hasn't necessarily "forgotten" something in the human sense. The information may simply no longer be available when the model generates its next response.

Character Machinery Needs to Be Efficient

If you're building complex characters, don't think:
"How much information can I put into the backend?"
Think:
"What information does the model actually need in order to produce the behavior I want?"
That's a completely different question.

For example:
Weak use of context:
Sarah was born in 1997 in a small town...

Potentially useful behavioral machinery:
Sarah uses humor when uncomfortable. She becomes defensive when confronted about her feelings. She wants {{user}}'s approval but refuses to openly ask for it.

The second example is much more likely to affect the next response.
Write for behavior, not trivia.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Different Models Have Different Limits
Not every LLM has the same context window.
A character that works beautifully on one model may behave completely differently on another.
You can have:
Model A — 16K context
Model B — 32K context
Model C — 128K context
Those aren't simply different levels of "smart."
They can have fundamentally different amounts of information available to them during a conversation.
And even when two models advertise the same context size, their instruction-following and information retrieval can still differ.
Model choice matters enormously for complex RP.
The Practical Rule
When deciding what information deserves space, prioritize it by how much it affects the character's actual behavior.
What must the character ALWAYS do?
→ Behavioral rules
Who is the character?
→ Personality
How does the character behave toward {{user}}?
→ Relationships
What is happening RIGHT NOW?
→ Scenario
What happened before the story began?
→ Backstory
Backstory isn't useless.
It's just not automatically the highest-value use of limited context.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Trim Your Backend to What Actually Matters
One of the hardest lessons to learn when building characters is:
Not everything that makes your character cool needs to be in the backend.
Creators naturally want the AI to know everything about their character.
But ask yourself:
"Does the LLM actually need this information to produce the next response?"
If the answer is no, you're potentially wasting context.
You might have three paragraphs explaining a character's childhood, family history, favorite foods, hometown, and everything else that happened before the RP begins.
That's interesting information.
But if none of it affects how the character behaves during the conversation, it probably doesn't deserve a large portion of your context budget.
Put the story where it belongs.
The First Message establishes the opening situation.
It can establish:
Where the RP begins
What is happening
The relationship between the characters
Immediate conflict
Tone
Relevant backstory
Why {{user}} is there
What the character currently wants
Two well-written paragraphs can communicate an enormous amount of information without permanently stuffing all of it into the character backend.
For example:
Sarah has been your girlfriend for seven months. Things were good until three weeks ago, when her ex returned to town. She hasn't told you they've been talking again. Tonight, you find her sitting alone at the bar where they first met...
That establishes relationship history, current conflict, and the starting situation in a tiny amount of text.
You don't necessarily need 2,000 tokens in the backend explaining the entire relationship.

messages.author: Dozer
messages.content:
Separate the Behavioral Engine From the Story
Think of your character as having two major components.
Behavioral Engine
How does this character behave?
Personality
Motivations
Fears
Contradictions
Behavioral rules
Speech patterns
Relationship behavior
Hard limits
Character-specific machinery
Response / Scenario Engine
What is happening right now?
First Message
Current situation
Immediate conflict
Setting
Tone
Relevant history
The behavioral engine should remain relatively stable.
The scenario can change.
That means you don't need to rebuild your character every time you put them into a different situation.
The character's behavior stays consistent while the story changes around them.
Character Consistency > Information Density
This is the biggest takeaway.
You don't want the LLM thinking:
"I know 4,000 facts about Sarah."
You want it thinking:
"I know how Sarah behaves."
If the backend establishes the behavioral engine and the First Message establishes the current scenario, you've given the model two things it actually needs:
How should I behave?
and
What am I responding to right now?
Everything else should earn its place.
The simplest trimming test:
Ask yourself:
"If I delete this sentence, will the character behave differently?"
If the answer is no, consider deleting it.
If the answer is yes, keep it.
That's how you turn a bloated character definition into a high-signal backend.
Instead of making your backend an encyclopedia:
Behavioral machinery → Backend
Current story → First Message / Scenario
User choices → Conversation
The less unnecessary information you force the model to carry, the more room it has to actually respond to the user and develop the story.
